+	balancer.SubConn
+
+	// "The subchannel wrappers created by the outlier_detection LB policy will
+	// hold a reference to its map entry in the LB policy, if that map entry
+	// exists." - A50
+	obj unsafe.Pointer // *object
+	// These two pieces of state will reach eventual consistency due to sync in
+	// run(), and child will always have the correctly updated SubConnState.
+	latestState balancer.SubConnState
+	ejected     bool

+	scUpdateCh *buffer.Unbounded
+

+// eject(): "The wrapper will report a state update with the TRANSIENT_FAILURE
+// state, and will stop passing along updates from the underlying subchannel."
+func (scw *subConnWrapper) eject() {
+	scw.scUpdateCh.Put(&ejectedUpdate{
+		scw:     scw,
+		ejected: true,
+	})
+}
+
+// uneject(): "The wrapper will report a state update with the latest update
+// from the underlying subchannel, and resume passing along updates from the
+// underlying subchannel."
+func (scw *subConnWrapper) uneject() {
+	scw.scUpdateCh.Put(&ejectedUpdate{
+		scw:     scw,
+		ejected: false,
+	})

To keep implementations similar, I think it's best to do it as such. Plus, there's 8 callsites for both of these methods and I think it's cleaner for scw.eject()/scw.uneject() instead of putting stuff on update channel for each call site. These are part of the balancer.Balancer API, which is guaranteed to be called synchronously. Every single other read (outside of the SubConn updates) are in the balancer.Balancer API, meaning there is a guarantee of no concurrent write to the child. handleSubConnUpdate/handleEjectedUpdate is not guaranteed to be synchronous with the balancer.Balancer API, so thus I protected the reads to child with the mutex, and also this is an atomic guarantee of behavior that protects against the scenario where 1. read child is not nil 2. Close() the child (nils it too) 3. UpdateSubConnState to Closed child, breaking the balancer API.

Picker updates need to happen as part of `UpdateClientConnState` and not asynchronously. We also need to inhibit any state updates from the child policies leading to picker updates when the parent is processing its config here. See: https://github.com/grpc/grpc-go/issues/5211. According to the gRFC:

```
Calculate the mean and standard deviation of the fractions of successful requests among
addresses with total request volume of at least success_rate_ejection.request_volume.
```

In that case, the denominator for the mean and variance should not be `len(b.addrs)`, but the number of addresses which have at least `requestVolume` number of requests.

If that is the case, I would refactor the success algorithm as follows:
- `addrsWithAtLeastRequestVolume` : return a slice of addresses which have at least request volume number of request
- `meanAndStdDev`: takes as input, the above slice
```golang
```
And in the above two funcs, consider creating a local var for `addrInfo.callCounter.inactiveBucket`, because otherwise the lines are long and require more effort to read.

I would suggest `s/ccb/bucket/` because `ccb` is widely used in our codebase as the clientconn balancer wrapper.

And `s/sre/ejectionCfg/` because the first thing that anyone thinks of when we see `sre` is Site Reliability Engineer :), and since we are in the context of the success rate algorithm, it should be totally fine to omit the success prefix from the `ejectionCfg`.

body: Thanks for the suggestion. I like the idea. A few caveats here. The ejected SubConns causing only a round robin across 1 and 2 will be unejected in ejection analysis sweeps. Thus, this isn't the asymptotic behavior, but is behavior that should happen at a certain part in time. Thus, I can have a function similar to yours in the other PR I reviewed, where it waits over a time period to get a situation where you get only 1 and 2's in picks. Michael's interop test setup 5 backends and essentially made sure the ejected backend stopped receiving load and when unejected and healthy, continues to receive load. I would want further discussion on this though, since such a change could introduce flakiness and a lot of effort. I wouldn't mind changing this though, either to your suggestion or another one we come up with. @dfawley

body:
> Right now, the interval timer algorithm (think interval being zero)/uneject all subconns in the case of flipping to a no-op config is guaranteed to read this new b.child as it is forwarding updates downward (b.UpdateSubConnState)

With the current state of the code, the following can happen:
- we receive the config, and close the old child policy and build the new one
- update the address map, and as part of that figure out that we have a no-op config, and hence uneject all previously ejected subConns
  - these will show up as subConnState updates on the new child

But we still haven't given the child it's configuration. We do that only in line 288. This doesn't seem right to me.

The gRFC states the following:
```
When the outlier_detection LB policy receives an address update, it will create a map entry
for each subchannel address in the list, and remove each map entry for a subchannel address
not in the list, then pass the address list along to the child policy.
```

The correct order then, it seems would be:
- update the address maps in the balancer based on the received update
- close the old child and create a new one if the child policy name has changed
- push the new config to the child
- do the stuff around stopping/starting the interval timer algorithm, unejecting addresses etc

According to the gRFC, this block of code should be done only if the config specifies at least one of the ejection algorithms. https://screenshot.googleplex.com/326HFc3hWjbFuPY.

You could probably simplify this code by adding a couple of helpers, one for the things to be done when a no-op config is specified, and one for the things to be done when a non-noop config is specified.

Why can't we do this inline? Why do we need to go through this channel? If we set `inhibitPickerUpdates` to `true` at the top of this function, any updates from child policies in the meantime would be dropped until we push a picker from here, and reset `inhibitPickerUpdates`.

body:
I'm generally in favor of testing functionality over testing state. And I would advice that most of these tests be rewritten so that they do not rely on testing any internal state. My experience is that tests written that way are much more maintainable, and offer much better return on investment over time.

Grabbing the lock from the test is definitely not something that I would be comfortable approving.

Saying the above calls to `pi.Done(balancer.DoneInfo{})` simulate successful RPC calls, while `pi.Done(balancer.DoneInfo{Err: errors.New("some error")})` simulate failed RPC calls. What value is this? `math.MaxInt64`? why not use that instead?

Would `if dur != 8 * time.Second { .. }` be better?

body: Thanks for all the suggestions. Unfortunately, you can't read the scw1 and scw2 off the tcc, as the sc forwarded to the tcc is not the wrapped SubConn, but the SubConn that the SubConn wrapper is wrapping. Thus, if you want to simulate an UpdateAddresses call from the child, you need to use the SubConn returned from Outlier Detection downward, as that is what the child will call UpdateAddresses with.
